text: You just stepped out into freezing wind, and your arms instantly turn bumpy like a plucked chicken.
Every hair on your body grows out of a tiny pocket in your skin.
And hooked to each one is a muscle so small you can't even see it.
When you get cold, your brain fires a signal down a nerve.
Thousands of those tiny muscles squeeze at the same time.
They yank every hair straight up and pull the skin into little bumps.
For a furry animal, that puffs up its coat to trap warm air, and it looks bigger too.
That's why a scared cat suddenly looks twice its size.
But you don't have much fur left, so you just get bumps.
Fear or a song you love can set it off too, using the same nerve.
And scientists found that squeeze can even wake up cells that help grow new hair.
Subscribe, because that's what really gives you goosebumps.
